Jenna Jambeck

bibl.title: Production, use, and fate of all plastics ever made

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: every mass-produced plastic ever manufactured - polymer resins, synthetic fibers and additives - from production through use to end-of-life fate, 1950 to 2015
span.quote: By identifying and synthesizing dispersed data on production, use, and end-of-life management of polymer resins, synthetic fibers, and additives, we present the first global analysis of all mass-produced plastics ever manufactured.

span.label: how much plastic has been made, how much is still in use, and where the rest of it went
span.quote: Plastics have outgrown most man-made materials and have long been under environmental scrutiny. However, robust global information, particularly about their end-of-life fate, is lacking.

span.label: the first global material-flow account of all mass-produced plastics, including fibers and additives, which had typically been omitted
span.quote: By identifying and synthesizing dispersed data on production, use, and end-of-life management of polymer resins, synthetic fibers, and additives, we present the first global analysis of all mass-produced plastics ever manufactured.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We estimate that 8300 million metric tons (Mt) as of virgin plastics have been produced to date. As of 2015, approximately 6300 Mt of plastic waste had been generated, around 9% of which had been recycled, 12% was incinerated, and 79% was accumulated in landfills or the natural environment.

span.label: the accumulation of non-biodegradable plastic waste in landfills and the natural environment
span.quote: The vast majority of monomers used to make plastics, such as ethylene and propylene, are derived from fossil hydrocarbons. None of the commonly used plastics are biodegradable. As a result, they accumulate, rather than decompose, in landfills or the natural environment

span.label: a material flow model combining production statistics with log-normal product lifetime distributions for eight use sectors, and regional recycling, incineration and discard rates
span.term: a material flow model combining production statistics with log-normal product lifetime distributions for eight use sectors, and regional recycling, incineration and discard rates
span.quote: We combined plastic production data with product lifetime distributions for eight different industrial use sectors, or product categories, to model how long plastics are in use before they reach the end of their useful lifetimes and are discarded

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: NON-BIODEGRADABILITY CONVERTS PRODUCTION DIRECTLY INTO STOCK: because none of the commonly used plastics biodegrade, waste accumulates rather than decomposes, so every tonne made is still somewhere unless it was burned
span.quote: The vast majority of monomers used to make plastics, such as ethylene and propylene, are derived from fossil hydrocarbons. None of the commonly used plastics are biodegradable. As a result, they accumulate, rather than decompose, in landfills or the natural environment

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE ONLY PERMANENT SINK IS THERMAL DESTRUCTION - combustion or pyrolysis. Recycling and landfill both keep the material in the system, which is why the accounting has an ever-growing discarded stock
span.quote: The only way to permanently eliminate plastic waste is by destructive thermal treatment, such as combustion or pyrolysis.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: RECYCLING ONLY REDUCES FUTURE WASTE IF IT DISPLACES PRIMARY PRODUCTION, and whether it does is counterfactual and so extremely difficult to establish - the mechanism is stated together with the reason it cannot be measured
span.note: status: because of its counterfactual nature, this displacement is extremely difficult to establish
span.quote: Recycling delays, rather than avoids, final disposal. It reduces future plastic waste generation only if it displaces primary plastic production ( _30_); however, because of its counterfactual nature, this displacement is extremely difficult to establish

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: MIXING AND CONTAMINATION DEGRADE THE SECONDARY MATERIAL, so recycled plastic is of limited or low technical and economic value and cannot simply substitute for virgin material
span.quote: Furthermore, contamination and the mixing of polymer types generate secondary plastics of limited or low technical and economic value.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SUNLIGHT FRAGMENTS RATHER THAN DEGRADES: weathering breaks the material into millimetre and micrometre particles without biodegrading it, which is where microplastics come from
span.quote: None of the mass-produced plastics biodegrade in any meaningful way; however, sunlight weakens the materials, causing fragmentation into particles known to reach millimeters or micrometers in size

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES PLASTIC USEFUL IS THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES IT PERSIST - durability and resistance to degradation are the same fact described from two sides, so the problem is not a defect in the material but its purpose
span.quote: The same properties that make plastics so versatile in innumerable applications—durability and resistance to degradation—make these materials difficult or impossible for nature to assimilate.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: PRODUCT LIFETIME DECOUPLES WASTE FROM PRODUCTION IN TIME: packaging leaves use the year it is made while construction plastic leaving use today was made decades ago, when volumes were far lower - so the waste stream's composition is not the production stream's
span.quote: Most of the packaging plastics leave use the same year they are produced, whereas construction plastics leaving use were produced decades earlier, when production quantities were much lower.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE SHIFT FROM REUSABLE TO SINGLE-USE CONTAINERS DROVE PACKAGING, the largest market, and packaging is the shortest-lived sector - so the market that grew fastest is the one that becomes waste soonest
span.quote: plastics’ largest market is packaging, an application whose growth was accelerated by a global shift from reusable to single-use containers.

span.label: the two largest sources of uncertainty are named: product-category lifetime distributions, and incineration and recycling rates outside Europe and the US
span.quote: The largest sources of uncertainty are the lifetime distributions of the product categories and the plastic incineration and recycling rates outside of Europe and the United States.

span.label: waste management data were sparse and of poor quality in many world regions, which is why the sensitivity analysis was run
span.quote: In many world regions, waste management data were sparse and of poor quality. For this reason, sensitivity analysis with regard to waste management rates was conducted.

span.label: the additives-to-polymer fraction and the sector breakdowns are known only for 2000-2014 and were assumed constant back to 1950
span.quote: Polymer type and industrial use sector breakdowns of polymer production and the additives to polymer fraction were both stable over the time period for which data are available and thus assumed constant throughout the modeling period of 1950–2015.

span.label: bio-based and biodegradable plastics are excluded from the analysis entirely, at a stated global capacity of 4 Mt
span.quote: Bio-based or biodegradable plastics currently have a global production capacity of only 4 Mt and are excluded from this analysis

span.label: the more direct measurement route - solid waste generation combined with waste characterization - was unavailable at the required detail and quality for many countries
span.quote: A more direct way to measure plastic waste generation is to combine solid waste generation data with waste characterization information, as in the study of Jambeck _et al._ ( _3_). However, for many countries, these data are not available in the detail and quality required for the present analysis.

span.label: end-of-life textiles are assumed to be incinerated and discarded with municipal solid waste, on the ground that there is no significant fiber recycling
span.quote: There is currently no significant recycling of synthetic fibers. It was thus assumed that end-of-life textiles are incinerated and discarded together with all other municipal solid waste.

span.label: the environmental impact of plastic waste in land-based ecosystems is stated to be largely unknown, in contrast to the marine and freshwater literature
span.quote: Research into the environmental impacts of these “microplastics” in marine and freshwater environments has accelerated in recent years ( _33_), but little is known about the impacts of plastic waste in land-based ecosystems.

span.label: fiber and additives production data are not readily available and had typically been omitted from previous analyses - which is the gap this paper fills and also the weakest part of its own inputs
span.quote: Data on fiber and additives production are not readily available and have typically been omitted until now.

span.label: the model's 2010 estimate was checked against an independently derived published estimate and matched it to within 1 Mt
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that the whole material-flow model is mis-specified - an independently derived published estimate for 2010 agrees to within 1 Mt (274 against 275) · outcome: held
span.quote: we estimate that plastic waste generation in 2010 was 274 Mt, which is equal to the independently derived estimate of 275 Mt by Jambeck _et al._

span.label: sensitivity analysis on product lifetimes: moving every category's mean by 1 SD moves cumulative primary waste generation by -4/+5%
span.note: eliminates: product lifetime assumptions as the driver of the headline totals - moving every category's mean by a full SD moves cumulative primary waste generation only -4/+5% · outcome: held
span.quote: Increasing/decreasing the mean lifetimes of all product categories by 1 SD changes the cumulative primary plastic waste generation (for 1950 to 2015) from 5900 to 4600/6200 Mt or by −4/+5%.

span.label: sensitivity analysis on waste management rates: moving incineration and recycling by 5 percentage points moves cumulative discarded waste by -8/+6%
span.note: eliminates: waste-management rates as the driver of the discarded-plastic total - moving incineration and recycling by 5 percentage points moves it only -8/+6% · outcome: held
span.quote: Increasing/decreasing current global incineration and recycling rates by 5%, and adjusting the time trends accordingly, changes the cumulative discarded plastic waste from 4900 (for 1950 to 2015) to 4500/5200 Mt or by −8/+6%.

span.label: the 2050 lines are declared forward projections of historical trends and NOT a prediction or forecast - the authors refuse the reading their own figure invites
span.note: eliminates: the reading that the 12,000 Mt-by-2050 figure is a forecast - it is declared a forward projection of historical trends and explicitly not a prediction · outcome: held
span.quote: The dashed lines in Fig. 3 are based on those assumptions and therefore simply forward projections of historical global trends and should not be mistaken for a prediction or forecast.

span.label: results are rounded to the nearest 100 Mt because the analysis is subject to considerable uncertainty - the precision of the reported number is itself chosen to match the uncertainty
span.note: eliminates: false precision - rounding to the nearest 100 Mt stops a reader treating the reported digits as resolved when the analysis carries considerable uncertainty · outcome: held
span.quote: Any material flow analysis of this kind requires multiple assumptions or simplifications, which are listed in Materials and Methods, and is subject to considerable uncertainty; as such, all cumulative results are rounded to the nearest 100 Mt.

span.label: additives production data are not publicly available and were bought from market research companies, then cross-checked for consistency
span.note: eliminates: a single commercial source being wrong or self-serving on the additives figures, which are not publicly available - they were cross-checked between providers · outcome: held
span.quote: Global additives production data, which are not publicly available, were acquired from market research companies and cross-checked for consistency

span.label: plastics
span.quote: We present the first global analysis of all mass-produced plastics ever made by developing and combining global data on production, use, and end-of-life fate of polymer resins, synthetic fibers, and additives into a comprehensive material flow model.

span.label: polymer resins
span.quote: We present the first global analysis of all mass-produced plastics ever made by developing and combining global data on production, use, and end-of-life fate of polymer resins, synthetic fibers, and additives into a comprehensive material flow model.

span.label: synthetic fibers
span.quote: We present the first global analysis of all mass-produced plastics ever made by developing and combining global data on production, use, and end-of-life fate of polymer resins, synthetic fibers, and additives into a comprehensive material flow model.

span.label: additives
span.quote: We present the first global analysis of all mass-produced plastics ever made by developing and combining global data on production, use, and end-of-life fate of polymer resins, synthetic fibers, and additives into a comprehensive material flow model.

span.label: material flow model
span.quote: We present the first global analysis of all mass-produced plastics ever made by developing and combining global data on production, use, and end-of-life fate of polymer resins, synthetic fibers, and additives into a comprehensive material flow model.

span.label: primary plastics
span.quote: We estimate that in 2015, 407 Mt of primary plastics (plastics manufactured from virgin materials) entered the use phase, whereas 302 Mt left it. Thus, in 2015, 105 Mt were added to the in-use stock.

span.label: secondary plastics
span.quote: Furthermore, contamination and the mixing of polymer types generate secondary plastics of limited or low technical and economic value.

span.label: recycling
span.quote: Global recycling and incineration rates have slowly increased to account for 18 and 24%, respectively, of nonfiber plastic waste generated in 2014

span.label: incineration
span.quote: Global recycling and incineration rates have slowly increased to account for 18 and 24%, respectively, of nonfiber plastic waste generated in 2014

span.label: discard rate
span.quote: With those two assumptions, global discard rate would decrease from 58% in 2014 to 6% in 2050

span.label: final disposal
span.quote: Recycling delays, rather than avoids, final disposal. It reduces future plastic waste generation only if it displaces primary plastic production ( _30_); however, because of its counterfactual nature, this displacement is extremely difficult to establish

span.label: microplastics
span.quote: Research into the environmental impacts of these “microplastics” in marine and freshwater environments has accelerated in recent years ( _33_), but little is known about the impacts of plastic waste in land-based ecosystems.

span.label: packaging
span.quote: plastics’ largest market is packaging, an application whose growth was accelerated by a global shift from reusable to single-use containers.

span.label: product lifetime distributions
span.quote: We combined plastic production data with product lifetime distributions for eight different industrial use sectors, or product categories, to model how long plastics are in use before they reach the end of their useful lifetimes and are discarded

span.label: log-normal distributions
span.quote: We assumed log-normal distributions with means ranging from less than 1 year, for packaging, to decades, for building and construction

span.label: sensitivity analysis
span.quote: In many world regions, waste management data were sparse and of poor quality. For this reason, sensitivity analysis with regard to waste management rates was conducted.

span.label: pyrolysis
span.quote: The only way to permanently eliminate plastic waste is by destructive thermal treatment, such as combustion or pyrolysis.

span.label: monomers
span.quote: The vast majority of monomers used to make plastics, such as ethylene and propylene, are derived from fossil hydrocarbons. None of the commonly used plastics are biodegradable. As a result, they accumulate, rather than decompose, in landfills or the natural environment

span.label: landfills
span.quote: The vast majority of monomers used to make plastics, such as ethylene and propylene, are derived from fossil hydrocarbons. None of the commonly used plastics are biodegradable. As a result, they accumulate, rather than decompose, in landfills or the natural environment

span.label: municipal solid waste
span.quote: There is currently no significant recycling of synthetic fibers. It was thus assumed that end-of-life textiles are incinerated and discarded together with all other municipal solid waste.

span.label: PP&A fibers
span.quote: On average, we find that nonfiber plastics contain 93% polymer resin and 7% additives by mass. When including additives in the calculation, the amount of nonfiber plastics (henceforth defined as resins plus additives) manufactured since 1950 increases to 7300 Mt. PP&A fibers add another 1000 Mt.

span.label: CAGR
span.quote: Global production of resins and fibers increased from 2 Mt in 1950 to 380 Mt in 2015, a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.4% (table S1), roughly 2.5 times the CAGR of the global gross domestic product during that period

span.label: primary plastics - IN THIS PAPER, PLASTIC MADE FROM VIRGIN MATERIAL, defined against `secondary` (recycled) rather than against any chemical property. The whole flow model turns on the distinction, because recycled material re-enters the use phase and would otherwise be counted twice
span.quote: We estimate that in 2015, 407 Mt of primary plastics (plastics manufactured from virgin materials) entered the use phase, whereas 302 Mt left it. Thus, in 2015, 105 Mt were added to the in-use stock.

span.label: recycling - EXPLICITLY A DELAY, NOT AN AVOIDANCE. The paper defines it by what it does to the flow: material returns to use and reaches final disposal later, and it only reduces future waste if it displaces primary production - which the paper says is extremely difficult to establish because the claim is counterfactual
span.quote: Recycling delays, rather than avoids, final disposal. It reduces future plastic waste generation only if it displaces primary plastic production ( _30_); however, because of its counterfactual nature, this displacement is extremely difficult to establish

span.label: plastic waste `fate` - A THREE-WAY EXHAUSTIVE PARTITION used as the model's accounting identity: recycled, thermally destroyed, or discarded. It is a bookkeeping category, not an environmental one - `discarded` covers both a sanitary landfill and the open ocean
span.quote: We estimate that 2500 Mt of plastics—or 30% of all plastics ever produced—are currently in use. Between 1950 and 2015, cumulative waste generation of primary and secondary (recycled) plastic waste amounted to 6300 Mt. Of this, approximately 800 Mt (12%) of plastics have been incinerated and 600 Mt (9%) have been recycled, only 10% of which have been recycled more than once. Around 4900 Mt—60% of all plastics ever produced—were discarded and are accumulating in landfills or in the natural environment

span.label: confirms → Jambeck et al.'s independently derived estimate of plastic waste generation, which this model reproduces to within 1 Mt (274 against 275 Mt for 2010)
span.quote: we estimate that plastic waste generation in 2010 was 274 Mt, which is equal to the independently derived estimate of 275 Mt by Jambeck _et al._

span.label: distinguishes-from → the direct method of combining solid waste generation data with waste characterization, which the authors could not use because the data are not available at the required detail and quality for many countries
span.quote: A more direct way to measure plastic waste generation is to combine solid waste generation data with waste characterization information, as in the study of Jambeck _et al._ ( _3_). However, for many countries, these data are not available in the detail and quality required for the present analysis.

span.label: recycling —distinct-from→ final disposal
span.quote: Recycling delays, rather than avoids, final disposal. It reduces future plastic waste generation only if it displaces primary plastic production ( _30_); however, because of its counterfactual nature, this displacement is extremely difficult to establish

span.label: primary plastics —distinct-from→ secondary plastics
span.quote: We estimate that 2500 Mt of plastics—or 30% of all plastics ever produced—are currently in use. Between 1950 and 2015, cumulative waste generation of primary and secondary (recycled) plastic waste amounted to 6300 Mt. Of this, approximately 800 Mt (12%) of plastics have been incinerated and 600 Mt (9%) have been recycled, only 10% of which have been recycled more than once. Around 4900 Mt—60% of all plastics ever produced—were discarded and are accumulating in landfills or in the natural environment

span.label: product lifetime distributions —operationalised-as→ log-normal distributions
span.quote: We assumed log-normal distributions with means ranging from less than 1 year, for packaging, to decades, for building and construction

span.label: additives —part-of→ plastics
span.quote: On average, we find that nonfiber plastics contain 93% polymer resin and 7% additives by mass. When including additives in the calculation, the amount of nonfiber plastics (henceforth defined as resins plus additives) manufactured since 1950 increases to 7300 Mt. PP&A fibers add another 1000 Mt.

span.label: monomers —part-of→ plastics
span.quote: The vast majority of monomers used to make plastics, such as ethylene and propylene, are derived from fossil hydrocarbons. None of the commonly used plastics are biodegradable. As a result, they accumulate, rather than decompose, in landfills or the natural environment

span.label: recycling delays rather than avoids final disposal, and reduces future waste only if it displaces primary production - which is counterfactual and extremely difficult to establish
span.quote: Recycling delays, rather than avoids, final disposal. It reduces future plastic waste generation only if it displaces primary plastic production ( _30_); however, because of its counterfactual nature, this displacement is extremely difficult to establish

span.label: the properties that make plastics versatile - durability and resistance to degradation - are the same ones that make them impossible for nature to assimilate
span.quote: The same properties that make plastics so versatile in innumerable applications—durability and resistance to degradation—make these materials difficult or impossible for nature to assimilate.

span.label: US plastic recycling has been flat at 9% since 2012 while Europe reached 30% and China 25% in 2014
span.quote: the highest recycling rates in 2014 were in Europe (30%) and China (25%), whereas in the United States, plastic recycling has remained steady at 9% since 2012

span.label: the share of plastics in municipal solid waste by mass rose from under 1% in 1960 to over 10% by 2005 in middle- and high-income countries
span.quote: the share of plastics in municipal solid waste (by mass) increased from less than 1% in 1960 to more than 10% by 2005 in middle- and high-income countries

span.label: 8300 Mt of virgin plastics produced to date; 6300 Mt of plastic waste generated as of 2015, 9% recycled, 12% incinerated, 79% accumulated — None
span.quote: We estimate that 8300 million metric tons (Mt) as of virgin plastics have been produced to date. As of 2015, approximately 6300 Mt of plastic waste had been generated, around 9% of which had been recycled, 12% was incinerated, and 79% was accumulated in landfills or the natural environment.

span.label: roughly 12,000 Mt of plastic waste in landfills or the natural environment by 2050 if trends continue — None
span.quote: If current production and waste management trends continue, roughly 12,000 Mt of plastic waste will be in landfills or in the natural environment by 2050.

span.label: production rose from 2 Mt in 1950 to 380 Mt in 2015, a CAGR of 8.4%, about 2.5 times the CAGR of global GDP over the same period — None
span.quote: Global production of resins and fibers increased from 2 Mt in 1950 to 380 Mt in 2015, a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.4% (table S1), roughly 2.5 times the CAGR of the global gross domestic product during that period

span.label: 7800 Mt of resins and fibers made 1950-2015, half of it in the last 13 years — None
span.quote: The total amount of resins and fibers manufactured from 1950 through 2015 is 7800 Mt. Half of this—3900 Mt—was produced in just the past 13 years.

span.label: 2500 Mt (30% of all plastics ever produced) still in use; 4900 Mt (60%) discarded and accumulating — None
span.quote: We estimate that 2500 Mt of plastics—or 30% of all plastics ever produced—are currently in use. Between 1950 and 2015, cumulative waste generation of primary and secondary (recycled) plastic waste amounted to 6300 Mt. Of this, approximately 800 Mt (12%) of plastics have been incinerated and 600 Mt (9%) have been recycled, only 10% of which have been recycled more than once. Around 4900 Mt—60% of all plastics ever produced—were discarded and are accumulating in landfills or in the natural environment

span.label: nonfiber plastics are 93% polymer resin and 7% additives by mass — None
span.quote: On average, we find that nonfiber plastics contain 93% polymer resin and 7% additives by mass. When including additives in the calculation, the amount of nonfiber plastics (henceforth defined as resins plus additives) manufactured since 1950 increases to 7300 Mt. PP&A fibers add another 1000 Mt.

span.label: seven polymer groups account for 92% of all plastics ever made — None
span.quote: The largest groups in total nonfiber plastics production are PE (36%), PP (21%), and PVC (12%), followed by PET, PUR, and PS (<10% each). Polyester, most of which is PET, accounts for 70% of all PP&A fiber production. Together, these seven groups account for 92% of all plastics ever made.

span.label: China accounts for 28% of global resin and 68% of global PP&A fiber production — None
span.quote: Today, China alone accounts for 28% of global resin and 68% of global PP&A fiber production

span.label: only 10% of recycled plastic has been recycled more than once — None
span.quote: approximately 800 Mt (12%) of plastics have been incinerated and 600 Mt (9%) have been recycled, only 10% of which have been recycled more than once.

span.label: the resin production series fits a second-order polynomial time trend at R2 = 0.9968 and the fiber series a third-order polynomial at R2 = 0.9934
span.quote: The resin data closely follow a second-order polynomial time trend, which generated a fit of _R_ 2 = 0.9968. The fiber data closely follow a third-order polynomial time trend, which generated a fit of _R_ 2 = 0.9934.

span.label: moving all mean product lifetimes by 1 SD changes cumulative primary plastic waste generation by -4/+5%
span.quote: Increasing/decreasing the mean lifetimes of all product categories by 1 SD changes the cumulative primary plastic waste generation (for 1950 to 2015) from 5900 to 4600/6200 Mt or by −4/+5%.

span.label: moving incineration and recycling rates by 5% changes cumulative discarded plastic waste by -8/+6%
span.quote: Increasing/decreasing current global incineration and recycling rates by 5%, and adjusting the time trends accordingly, changes the cumulative discarded plastic waste from 4900 (for 1950 to 2015) to 4500/5200 Mt or by −8/+6%.

span.label: product lifetime by industrial use sector, under 1 year for packaging to decades for building and construction
span.term: product lifetime by industrial use sector, under 1 year for packaging to decades for building and construction
span.quote: We assumed log-normal distributions with means ranging from less than 1 year, for packaging, to decades, for building and construction

span.label: global recycling, incineration and discard rates by region and year
span.term: global recycling, incineration and discard rates by region and year
span.quote: Global recycling and incineration rates have slowly increased to account for 18 and 24%, respectively, of nonfiber plastic waste generated in 2014
